## The Setting

- Linear regression is an inferential (and therefore, relatively inflexible) model in which we assume that $Y$ is related to the predictor variables $\mathbf{x}$ via the model 
$$Y \mid \mathbf{x} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p + \epsilon$$

  + $\epsilon$ represents the scatter of data around the regression line

- Today, let's start by pointing out a likely pretty obvious fact:

  + just because a predictor variable exists in your data table doesn't mean that it has predictive power!

- In variable selection, we attempt to select a subset $s$ out of the $p$ overall predictors in a linear model

  + this **will** *improve model interpretability*; eliminating uninformative predictors is obviously a good thing when your goal is to tell the story of how your predictors are associated with your response

  + this **can** *improve prediction accuracy*; eliminating uninformative predictors can lead to lower model *variance*, at the expense of a slight increase in *bias*, but ultimately leading to lower test-set mean-squared error values

- Note that variable selection (or some other adjustment, which we'll also discuss) is not just useful, but **necessary** if, $n < p$ (i.e., the sample size is less than the number of predictor variables), but can still be helpful if $n \gtrsim p$, particularly when $n \approx p$ 


---

## Best Subset Selection

.center[
  ![:scale 50%](./Algorithm_6.1.png)
]

(Algorithm 6.1, *Introduction to Statistical Learning* by James et al.)

<br>

- Note that:

$${p \choose k} = \frac{p!}{k!(p-k)!}$$

- For multiple linear regression, BSS works for $p \lesssim 25$, but for larger $p$, computer memory quickly becomes an issue


---

## Best Subset Selection: Metrics

- The functional forms of the metrics given in Step 3 are

\begin{eqnarray*}
C_p &=& \frac{{\rm RSS} + 2k\widehat{\sigma}^2}{n} \\[0.2em]
{\rm AIC} &=& \frac{{\rm RSS} + 2k \widehat{\sigma}^2}{n \widehat{\sigma}^2} = \frac{C_p}{\widehat{\sigma}^2} \\[0.2em]
{\rm BIC} &=& \frac{{\rm RSS} + \log(n)k\widehat{\sigma}^2}{n}
\end{eqnarray*}

- ${\rm RSS}$ denotes the "residual sum-of-squares"

- **KEY:** all the additive terms are penalty terms that increase with $k$ and thus act to prevent overfitting 

- $\widehat{\sigma}$ is an estimate of the standard deviation of the error term $\epsilon$, i.e., the magnitude of the scatter of data around the regression line


---

## Best Subset Selection: Metrics

- Typically, $\log(n) > 2$, so the BIC (or "Bayesian Information Criterion") imposes a larger penalty relative to the $C_p$ (or "Mallow's $C_p$") or the AIC (or "Akaike Information Criterion")

- Relative to each other:

  + BIC tends to underfit (i.e., it will select as optimal those models that have *fewer* variables)

  + AIC (and $C_p$) tend to overfit (i.e., they will select models with *more* variables)

- Which metric you choose is up to you - there's no *right* answer; the choice should be motivated by your inferential goals:

  + if you use BIC, then you can be confident that every selected variable is informative, but other informative variables might have been left out of the final list

  + if you use AIC, then you can be confident that your selected variables include all the informative ones, but the final list may also include some uninformative ones as well


---

## Forward and Backward Stepwise Selection

- What if BSS is computationally infeasible?

- In that case, we might use either *forward* or *backward stepwise selection*; e.g., the former:

.center[
  ![:scale 50%](./Algorithm_6.2.png)
]

(Algorithm 6.2, *Introduction to Statistical Learning* by James et al.)


---

## Forward and Backward Stepwise Selection

- In words:

  + forward stepwise selection starts with no predictor variables and adds one at a time
  
  + backward stepwise selection starts with the full set of predictors and takes one away at a time

- Forward and backward stepwise selection are examples of *greedy algorithms*: they make locally optimally choices which, collectively, **may not yield** a globally optimal solution

  + BSS is always preferred, if applying it is computationally feasible

- Note that even when applied to the same dataset, forward and backward stepwise selection *can* yield very different results, although for datasets with relatively small $p$, results *tend* to be more similar


---

## Regression Example

```{r echo=FALSE}
load(url("https://github.com/FSKoerner/F25-36600-data/raw/refs/heads/main/photo_morph.Rdata"))
df <- data.frame(predictors, "y" = response)
```

- Below, `df` is a data frame with 3,419 rows and 17 columns

```{r warning=FALSE}
suppressMessages(library(bestglm))
set.seed(404)
train    <- sample(nrow(df), 0.7 * nrow(df))   # Perform 70-30 data splitting
df.train <- df[train, ]
df.test  <- df[-train, ]
lm.out   <- lm(y ~ ., data = df.train)         # Response variable must be called "y" for the bestglm function
mse.full <- mean((predict(lm.out, newdata = df.test) - df.test$y)^2)
bg.out   <- bestglm(df.train, family = gaussian, IC = "BIC")
bg.out$BestModel
```

- We observe that 9 (or 11) of 16 predictor variables are retained when using BIC (or if we used the AIC) as the penalizing criterion


---

## Regression Example

```{r fig.height=4,fig.width=5,fig.align="center"}
library(ggplot2)
df.bg        <- data.frame(1:16, bg.out$Subsets$BIC[-1])   # The -1 gets rid of the BIC for the s = 0 model
names(df.bg) <- c("p", "BIC")
g            <- ggplot(data = df.bg, mapping = aes(x = p, y = BIC)) + 
                  geom_point() + geom_line() + 
                  ylim(min(df.bg$BIC), min(df.bg$BIC) + 200)
suppressWarnings(print(g))
```


---

## Regression Example

- The output of `bestglm()` contains the element `BestModel` 

  + `BestModel` is an "lm-object representing the best fitted algorithm" 
  
  + we can pass it to the `predict()` function in order to generate predicted response values
  
```{r}
resp.pred <- predict(bg.out$BestModel, newdata = df.test)
mean((df.test$y - resp.pred)^2)
# The saved value for the full predictor set that we calculated earlier:
mse.full
```

- In this case, removing the seven least important variables **improved** our predictive accuracy, albeit slightly


---

## Regression Example

- Now let's repeat the analysis, but with forward-stepwise selection:

```{r}
bg.out    <- bestglm(df.train, family = gaussian, IC = "BIC", method = "forward")
bg.out$BestModel
```

- This is a separate set of nine variables relative to the set produced by BSS, though there is a *fair bit* of overlap

```{r}
resp.pred <- predict(bg.out$BestModel, newdata = df.test)
mean((df.test$y - resp.pred)^2)   # Worse than for BSS or even the full set!
```
